title: Why Do Bees Matter?
paragraphs: Bees are popularly associated with honey, yet their ecological and economic significance lies overwhelmingly in pollination. In foraging for nectar and pollen, they transfer pollen between flowers, enabling the fertilisation on which the reproduction of countless plant species depends.

The managed honeybee, moreover, represents only a fraction of this work. Roughly 20,000 bee species have been described, and wild species, from bumblebees to solitary mining bees, are frequently more effective at pollinating particular crops. A diverse cast of other animals, including hoverflies, butterflies, birds and bats, also plays a part.

International scientific assessments suggest that some three quarters of the world’s leading food crops benefit, at least to some extent, from animal pollination. Although staple cereals such as wheat, rice and maize are wind-pollinated, many of the fruits, vegetables, nuts and seeds that supply essential micronutrients rely substantially on pollinators, as do valuable commodities like coffee and cocoa.

There is mounting evidence that many pollinator populations are in decline. The causes are multiple and interacting: the loss and fragmentation of habitat, the spread of intensive monocultures, exposure to certain pesticides, pathogens and parasites, and climate change, which can desynchronise flowering times from the activity of the insects that depend on them. Conservation therefore requires action on several fronts, from restoring flower-rich habitats to reforming agricultural practice.
